title: Heaven (CCC 1023–1029)
hookLine: seeing God face to face, beyond what eye has seen

cards: Clouds. Harps. Everyone in white robes, a bit bored, forever.
That's the cartoon heaven, and no wonder some call it dull. Set a different scene next to it. An airport arrivals gate, late at night.
The doors slide open, and someone you love, someone you haven't seen in years, comes around the corner. Your eyes meet. For one second the noise of the hall drops away.
Catholic teaching about heaven has almost nothing to do with the clouds and everything to do with that second: a face, seen at last, and never lost again.

teach.h: THROUGH A GLASS, THEN FACE TO FACE.
teach.b: Paul writes, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Now the seeing is dim, like a reflection in a glass. Then, direct.
First John adds: "we shall see him as he is."
The Church calls this seeing the beatific vision, from the Latin visio beatifica: the vision that makes you happy.

The Catechism describes heaven as perfect life with the Trinity, a communion of life and love with God, Mary, the angels and all the blessed. It calls heaven the fulfillment of the deepest longings of the human heart.

Augustine said it at the start of his Confessions: "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." Heaven, for Catholics, is that rest. The Catechism admits this mystery goes beyond any understanding or description.
So Scripture uses pictures: life, light, peace, a wedding feast, the Father's house, a city.
Paul reaches for an older scripture: "That eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man, what things God hath prepared for them that love him."
Each image points somewhere; none is enough on its own.

teach.h: OUR HEART IS RESTLESS, UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.
teach.b: Seeing God, Catholics say, isn't staring at a wall forever. Some Catholic writers describe it as endless discovery of one who has no end, shared with all the blessed.
Face to face with God, and so, many Catholics hope, face to face again with those they've lost.

how: Catholics pray for the dead that they may see God's face, keep All Saints Day on November 1 for all who are in heaven, and at funerals the Church sings In Paradisum, asking that the angels lead the dead into paradise.

o: a vision of heaven given to saints on earth
the clouds and harps of the life to come
seeing God directly, as he is, in heaven

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: the Catechism describes heaven as clouds and harps
it calls heaven perfect life with the Trinity, and says Scripture's images point beyond words.
Paul says that now we see God clearly
now we see through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face.
the Catechism admits heaven is beyond description

games.q: Paul compares how we know God now with how we'll know him then. what picture does he use?
o: a dim mirror, then face to face.
games.why: we see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've lost, to death or to distance, and picture them coming toward you, at the arrivals gate, a kitchen door, a field: their face, the way they'd say your name.
Let yourself feel it, even if it aches; Catholics hope for this and more, that every good meeting is a hint of seeing God. If you pray, thank God for that person.

wordCard.voice: Beatific vision. From the Latin for the vision that makes happy: seeing God face to face, which Catholics believe is the heart of heaven. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the beatific vision, the sight of God that makes one happy.

carryVoice: Your line: face to face. No more dim glass. Three hundred twenty-eight days in, and still climbing.
